      <title>UK government promises disabled air passengers better safeguards</title>
      <link>https://www.theguardian.com/business/2026/oct/19/uk-government-promises-disabled-air-passengers-better-safeguards</link>
      <description><p>Despite recent progress, almost a fifth of air travellers with disabilities are still dissatisfied with their experience</p><p>Disabled passengers will have better safeguards when flying, the government has pledged, including protection from damaged wheelchairs and support from trained staff.</p><p>A report from an industry-led accessibility group said there was “much more to be done” but progress was being made, a year after a <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/world/2025/jul/16/uk-taskforce-calls-for-disability-training-for-all-airline-and-airport-staff">review led by Tanni Grey-Thompson</a> demanded action to improve air travel in response to <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/society/2022/jun/22/disabled-passengers-bearing-brunt-of-travel-disruption-say-charities">numerous incidents</a> in which passengers had been <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/society/2022/jun/06/disabled-woman-left-on-plane-at-gatwick-airport-for-an-hour-and-a-half">left stranded</a> without assistance.</p> <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/business/2026/oct/19/uk-government-promises-disabled-air-passengers-better-safeguards">Continue reading...</a></description>

      <description><p>When we can’t even afford to rent or buy somewhere to live, we have to ask: did we give the financial sector too much power?</p><ul><li><p>Leilani Farha is the former UN special rapporteur on adequate housing</p></li></ul><p>In the summer of 2021, I visited a homeless community in a park in Toronto, Canada, and spoke to one of the residents. And he captured something experienced by ordinary people around the world: the growing conviction that the housing system is no longer tethered to their needs. What he was pointing at is not just a housing crisis. It is a crisis of democracy.</p><p>Leilani Farha is the 2026 CBC Massey lecturer. This piece is based on her new book: <a href="https://guardianbookshop.com/housing-inc-9781487014285/">Housing Inc.: A Global Takeover and Our Fight for Home</a>. She is the former UN special rapporteur on adequate housing and the global director of the international human rights organisation, <a href="https://maketheshift.org/">The Shift</a></p> <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfree/2026/oct/19/housing-crisis-global-democracy-nations-financial-sector">Continue reading...</a></description>

      <description><p>Are they put off by the hen parties, the tea rooms or the £5-an-hour parking? No matter. The <a href="https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/ckd6dvjn681lo">BBC reports</a> January-to-June visitor numbers to my home town fell 8% compared with 2025, with visits to city attractions down by 17%.</p><p>This inspires a cocktail of conflicting emotions – selfish relief, a bit of huffiness (how dare they reject the birthplace of the Chocolate Orange <em>and </em>the KitKat?) and consternation. Our main economic activities in 2026 are “dressing up”, “tea and cake”, and “hen/stag night services (sub-categories: booze, kebabs, feather boas)”.       <title>Move over, pervert glasses – the latest toxic trend is robogroping</title>
      <link>https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfree/2026/oct/17/smartglasses-robogroping-toxic-trends</link>
      <description><p>Whenever a new technology is created, it will, without exception, immediately be used to harass girls and women</p><p>You may be familiar with <a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rule_34">rule 34</a> of the internet, which states that if something exists or can be imagined, there will almost certainly be online porn of it. Now let me introduce my rule 35: whenever a new technology is created, it will, without exception, immediately be used to harass girls and women.</p><p>See, for example, Meta’s “<a href="https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfree/2026/aug/31/law-meta-pervert-glasses-mockery">pervert glasses</a>”. As anyone could have foreseen, putting a tiny camera and microphone into smartglasses would immediately lead to people using them to record and harass women. Lo and behold, that is exactly what happened. So-called manfluencers have <a href="https://www.cnn.com/2026/02/09/world/manfluencers-smart-glasses-intl">filmed themselves</a> trying to flirt with women in public spaces and then uploaded the footage to TikTok. The women in these videos are often not aware they’ve been recorded until their identities are shared online and they are <a href="https://www.404media.co/meta-ray-ban-smart-glasses-pov-instagram-pickup-artists/">harassed</a> by strangers. And what’s Meta doing about this? It’s instituted a few bans and made some privacy updates, but doesn’t seem to have an appetite to properly solve the problem. Indeed, at the Meta Connect 2026 keynote, Mark Zuckerberg did <a href="https://www.tomsguide.com/computing/smart-glasses/what-was-missing-from-meta-connect-2026-an-apology">not feel the need</a> to apologize to the women whose lives have been upended by his technology.</p> <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfree/2026/oct/17/smartglasses-robogroping-toxic-trends">Continue reading...</a></description>

      <link>https://www.theguardian.com/world/ng-interactive/2026/oct/18/invisible-clear-air-turbulence-airline-safety-climate-crisis</link>
      <description><p>As the planet warms, airlines are grappling with what this means for air travel – and for the passengers who simply refuse to keep their seatbelts fastened</p><p>It was a swelteringly hot afternoon in south-west Myanmar on 21 May 2024. Tropical thunderstorms, showers and highs of 36C were forecast for the area around the Irrawaddy Basin. High above, monsoonal heat and humidity were building into a vast convective column of water vapour, a towering cumulonimbus cloud soaring up to 35,000ft (more than 10,500 metres) into the air. From the ground, it would have looked like something from a children’s picture book – a soft, fluffy white mass. But for Singapore Airlines flight SQ321 passing just above, it was anything but benign.</p><p>In the cabin of the Boeing 777, passengers were being woken up for breakfast with three hours to go on the journey from London to Singapore. For the 210 travellers on board, the past 10 hours had been uneventful. The seatbelt signs were off. Some were milling around, others were using the toilets, and cabin staff were preparing trolleys for service. At 2.19pm and 23 seconds local time, moderate turbulence shook the plane for 17 seconds and the seatbelt sign was switched on. Then, as one passenger described it, it was “like a grenade had gone off”. In just 4.6 seconds, any passenger not strapped in hit the roof with 1.5 times the force of gravity and was thrown back on the floor in an instant.</p> <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/world/ng-interactive/2026/oct/18/invisible-clear-air-turbulence-airline-safety-climate-crisis">Continue reading...</a></description>

      <description><p>For more than three decades, Michael Gove has been a leading figure in British Conservatism. As a journalist, government minister and now editor of the Tory bible, the Spectator, he has helped shape the right even as it has moved further rightwards. In the latest episode of Radical Thinking, Gove joins Aditya Chakrabortty to discuss the future of the right, his record on Brexit and austerity, and the Spectator’s position on Islam</p><p>Watch the full episode with Michael Gove <a href="https://youtu.be/cIGXagkUFr8">here</a>.
 <br>
 <br>
 Aditya’s suggested reading:</p><p>To read the fruits of Michael Gove’s dalliance with the Marxism Today gang, look up his essay in a 1998 collection called The Moderniser’s Dilemma: Radical Politics in the Age of Blair</p><p>For slalom ride through Michael Gove’s years in power, read <a href="https://www.lrb.co.uk/the-paper/v41/n17/richard-j.-evans/the-demented-dalek">The Demented Dalek</a> by the historian Richard J Evans in the London Review of Books</p><p>To learn more on what’s become of the British right, there’s a <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfree/2024/sep/12/tory-leadership-jenrick-tugendhat-cleverly-badenoch">column by me </a>for the Guardian</p><p>Just why the most successful political party is now failing is analysed in-depth by Phil Burton-Cartledge in his book <a href="https://guardianbookshop.com/the-partys-over-9781839760372/">The Party’s Over: The Rise and Fall of the Conservatives from Thatcher to Sunak</a></p><p>Phil also writes a very good blog on British politics, which keeps a close eye on how each party is trying to marshall a coalition of voters. <a href="https://averypublicsociologist.blogspot.com/2026/10/the-clear-blue-water-strategy.html">Here</a> he is on Kemi Badenoch</p><p>Geoffrey Wheatcroft does an entertaining short narrative in <a href="https://guardianbookshop.com/bloody-panico-9781804295755/">Bloody Panico!:</a></p><p><a href="https://guardianbookshop.com/bloody-panico-9781804295755/">or, Whatever Happened to The Tory Party</a></p><p>For more on the economics of the Cameron years, <a href="https://foundationaleconomy.com/wp-content/uploads/2017/01/wp87.pdf">this paper</a> is acute on how the Tories failed to move the UK away from being a country of renters towards a country of makers. Two of its authors will join us for a podcast later in the series.</p><p>And if you want to read how Brexit may have cost the UK 8% of GDP, there’s <a href="https://www.nber.org/papers/w34459?st_source=ai_overview">this paper</a> based on data from the Bank of England</p><p>Finally, on the Spectator read Nesrine Malik’s recent column in The Guardian</p><p><a href="https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfree/2026/jul/20/islamophobia-spectator-britain-oldest-political-magazine">Why has Britain’s oldest political magazine become such a rabid cheerleader for Islamophobia?</a></p> <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/politics/commentisfree/audio/2026/oct/17/austerity-is-inevitably-painful-how-michael-gove-justifies-his-politics-radical-thinking-with-aditya-chakrabortty-podcast">Continue reading...</a></description>
